title: Optical Coherence Tomography Based Biomechanical Fluid-Structure Interaction Analysis of Coronary Atherosclerosis Progression
protocol: Match baseline and OCT follow-up images using anatomical landmarks.
Analyze matched images between identified landmarks.
Load each OCT image into the image digitizer.
Mark points at the catheter center point and limits of the scale.
Export marked points for later use.
Manually mark the edge of the lumen, starting from the same location in every image.
Capture the curves of the lumen accurately.
Leave a gap at the catheter artefact.
Export files in .dat format.
Repeat this process for every OCT image.
Extract the outer wall in high attenuation regions using visible parts of the outer elastic membrane.
Fit an ellipse manually to estimate the outer wall location.
Click and drag the left mouse button to define the ellipse and position it appropriately.
Manually define the lipid arc, calculated to the lumen centroid.
Click and drag angle measures to define the lipid arc.
Manually define the fibrous cap thickness by clicking and dragging distance measures.
Import the overlaid images into the image digitizer.
Select the outer wall points using the fitted ellipse as a guide in regions of high attenuation where the outer elastic membrane is not visible.
Export the selected points to a .dat format.
Similarly, manually select the lipid surface starting from the same end of the lipid in every case.
Use the outer wall ellipsoidal guide for a consistent backside arc when selecting lipids.
Select and export the lipid surface points to a .dat file.
Leave a gap across the guidewire artefact as described.
Load the first angiographic image in the image digitizer.
Select the edges of the catheter to scale the image in later steps.
Manually mark the catheter centerline beginning with the proximal marker and moving distally, with evenly spaced points.
Export the data to .dat format.
Repeat for the second angiographic plane.
Load the data files that were exported in step 1.4.
Use the first two points to scale the data to millimeters.
Subtract the proximal data point from the remaining points in each dataset so that the curve begins at the origin of the coordinate system.
Generate rotation matrices for each angiographic view using angles θ and Φ.
Multiply the rotation matrices together.
Multiply the resultant matrix with the coordinates of each point from step 2.1.1 to obtain Pt3D.
Calculate the normal vector to each angiographic plane by multiplying x and y rotation matrices with the unit z-vector.
Project each point normal to its respective plane from proximal to distal location.
Calculate the midpoint of the shortest distance between projections for each point.
Use the 'interparc' function to divide the three-dimensional centerline into equally spaced points.
Ensure spacing between points equals the spacing between OCT images, determined by pullback speed.
Convert each OCT cross-section from pixels to mm using the scaling file.
Subtract the catheter center point from all cross-section points to center them about the catheter location.
Calculate the normal vector by subtracting the three-dimensional centerline point from the next distal point along the catheter curve.
Determine the rotation matrix components based on the normal vector calculated.
Multiply the scaled data points by the rotation matrix to align the OCT cross-section perpendicular to the catheter centerline.
Add the three-dimensional centerline point to all rotated points in the cross-section for positioning in three-dimensional space.
Repeat steps for every cross-section, including lumen, artery, and lipid sections.
Export the cross-sections to a text file for CAD software import.
Import the text files containing cross-sections into the 3D modeling software.
Click on the concept drop-down box and select 3D curve.
Generate the curves by clicking Generate.
Select all the curves in order and loft them together to create a solid component, ensuring add frozen is selected.
Create separate solids for the lumen, lipids, and outer wall, ensuring merge topology is enabled.
Omit a small mid-section lipid due to its size and computational cost.
Subtract the lumen and lipids from the artery wall using a Boolean operation, with the wall as the target body and lipids/lumen as tool bodies.
Share topology between the wall and lipids manually by highlighting them and right clicking to form a new part.
Create profiles that describe the pulsatile blood velocity and pressure by compiling User Defined Functions (UDF).
Model transient profiles measured from human patients in the literature as a Fourier series.
Mathematically describe the profiles using: imgsrc://cloudfront.jove.com/files/ftp_upload/62933/62933eq05.jpg
Fit coefficients a0-11, b1-11 to profiles described in the literature.
Use the first 11 terms for the Fourier series representation.
Write the profiles to a C formatted file using an integrated development environment such as Microsoft Visual Studio.
Apply outlet pressure as a flat profile.
Apply inlet velocity as a fully developed parabolic profile.
Ensure inlet velocity and pressure are sufficient to reproduce realistic conditions.
Enter engineering data and add a new material called artery.
Drag density and the 5-parameter Mooney-Rivlin model to the new material.
Set the density of the artery to 1,000 kg/m3.
Set the hyperelastic coefficients for the artery based on intima properties from literature.
Repeat adding a new material for lipid.
Drag density and the 5-parameter Mooney-Rivlin model to the new lipid material.
Set the density of the lipid to 1,000 kg/m3.
Set the hyperelastic coefficients for the lipid based on lipid properties from literature.
Suppress the lumen/fluid component by right clicking and selecting Suppress.
Assign the previously defined artery material to the artery solid.
Check if the units are appropriate for the artery material.
Assign the previously defined lipid material to the lipid solid.
Check if the units are appropriate for the lipid material.
Mesh the geometry using adaptive meshing with a target size of 0.14 mm.
Set the physics preference to nonlinear mechanical.
Adjust the mesh preferences to obtain reasonable mesh skewness values.
Ensure at least two to three mesh elements across gaps such as the fibrous cap.
Conduct a mesh independence study by gradually decreasing mesh size and comparing results until variation is less than 2%.
Check mesh skewness and adjust parameters like mesh size, growth rate, maximum size, or curvature angle if necessary.
Click on Analysis settings.
Turn automatic time stepping off for FSI simulations.
Set the number of substeps to one.
Set the simulation end time to 0.8 seconds (for a patient heart rate of 75 bpm).
Set the solver type to program controlled.
Choose either the direct or iterative method for solving.
Select full Newton-Raphson method.
Insert a fluid-solid interface under the Transient tab.
Specify the inner wall of the artery for the interface.
Pass data between the structure and fluid at the specified location.
Right-click under the Transient tab and insert displacements.
Duplicate displacements for x, y, and z directions.
Select function in the direction drop-down list.
Copy displacement functions extracted previously.
Enter the Model tab and check the units.
Suppress the artery and lipid part, leaving only the fluid domain.
Specify mesh metrics for the fluid domain.
Generate the mesh and check skewness.
Adjust element size, growth rate, refinement or curvature as needed.
Create named selections for the inlet, outlet, and wall surfaces.
Enable double precision in the Setup tab.
Set Solver type to Pressure Based.
Ensure Time is set to Transient.
Enable the k-omega Viscous Turbulence model.
Enable Shear Stress Transport and Low Reynolds Corrections.
Enter the command '/define/models/viscous/turbulence-expert/turb-non-newtonian?' in the command console.
Respond with 'yes' when prompted to enable nonlinear viscosity models.
Rename the fluid as blood under Materials.
Set a density of 1,050 kg/m³ for blood.
Select non-Newtonian power law for the viscosity model.
Set the Power-Law non-Newtonian consistency index, k, to 0.035.
Set the power law index, n, to 0.6.
Compile the user-defined function containing transient blood velocity and pressure.
Check the command lines for any errors.
Load the UDF by entering the User Defined tab.
Navigate to the directory of the UDF and import it.
Click on Build, then Load.
Check the console text carefully for errors or warnings.
Ensure no errors appear in the console.
Apply UDF names from the console to the inlet and outlet boundaries.
Select the Boundary Conditions tab.
Double-click on Inlet and choose the inlet UDF from the profile drop-down list.
Repeat the step to define the outlet pressure with the outlet UDF.
Enable the dynamic mesh by checking the tick box under the Dynamic Mesh tab.
Include smoothing, remeshing, and 6° of freedom solver tick boxes.
Set the diffusion parameter to 1.5.
Ensure maximum and minimum scales are within the limits of the mesh zone.
Set the target skewness to 0.7.
Show mesh properties by clicking on the Mesh Properties tab.
Create a new dynamic mesh zone.
Specify the wall of the lumen in the Region drop down list.
Select System Coupling for data passing to the artery component.
Create deforming mesh zones for the inlet, outlet, and interior lumen.
Enable remeshing and smoothing for each zone.
Set appropriate values for the mesh scales.
Check for negative cell volume errors and adjust mesh scales if needed.
Set the pressure-velocity coupling to coupled in the Methods tab.
Select second order for transient formulation and spatial discretization schemes.
Enter a Courant number of two in controls.
Set residual convergence criteria in the Monitors tab to 1e-5 for continuity and 1e-6 for other parameters.
Enter a Courant number of two under the courant number section in the Controls tab.
Select custom field functions under the Parameters and Customization tab.
Insert a new function by right clicking and selecting New.
Define a local normalized helicity (LNH) using the drop-down list of solver variables.
Set the number of timesteps to 160 in the Run Calculation tab.
Set the time step size to 5 ms in the Run Calculation tab.
Set the number of iterations to 300 in the Run Calculation tab.
Set the end time to 0.8 s in Analysis Settings.
Enter a timestep of 0.005 s in Analysis Settings.
Set the maximum iterations to 10.
Select the wall from the fluid component and the solid interface from the structural component.
Hold Ctrl and select both fluid-structure interfaces.
Right-click and create a data transfer between the fluid and structural components.
Adjust under-relaxation or ramping of the force being transferred from fluid to structure if necessary.
Update the settings when ready to run.
